_meta.methodology:
HOW THE HAZARD TABLE WAS BUILT

Sub-region keying. 24 keys: 14 coastal (the 11 the brief named, plus CT southeast shore, RI Newport/Aquidneck, and MA Islands, which behave differently enough from their neighbors that folding them in would hide the worst cases) and 10 interior/inland for contrast. Keys mirror the climate table's granularity so the two can be joined on subregion.

Field definitions, so the enums are auditable.
- surge_flood_risk: the SUBREGION-MODAL rating for coastal-adjacent residential stock, not the worst parcel. "high" = extensive VE/AE frontage and a documented historical surge or repetitive-loss record. "moderate" = real but geographically confined SFHA exposure (mostly barrier/sand-beach pockets on an otherwise rocky or elevated coast). "low" = riverine/pluvial only. MA North Shore, ME Casco Bay and ME southern coast are the interesting "moderate" calls: they are honestly less surge-exposed than everything south of Cape Cod because they lack the Buzzards Bay / Narragansett Bay / western-Long-Island-Sound funnel geometry, and their coasts are largely ledge. The notes flag their high-risk pockets explicitly so a parcel-level screen still catches Plum Island, Salisbury, Winthrop and Old Orchard Beach.
- insurance_climate: measured by market STRUCTURE, not by premium level. "crisis" is reserved for where the residual market has become the primary market - only MA Cape Cod and MA Islands qualify, on the hard evidence that the FAIR Plan is now the largest insurer there with roughly 4 in 10 homes on the plan. "strained" = documented non-renewals, voluntary-market withdrawal from waterfront, or a growing residual pool (all coastal CT/RI, coastal MA outside Cape/Islands, NH Seacoast, both ME coastal subregions). "normal" = ordinary voluntary market, flat dollar deductibles, no residual-market pressure - all ten interior subregions.
- wind_deductible: I distinguish STATUTORY regimes (MA, RI, CT all have named-storm/hurricane percentage deductibles; RI caps at 5% by RIGL 27-76) from CARRIER-IMPOSED ones (NH and ME, which are not on the standard hurricane-deductible-state list - percentage wind deductibles there appear by underwriting choice, vary more, and are more negotiable). This distinction matters for a screen because the statutory-state deductible is effectively non-negotiable on a VE parcel.
- seasonality: "heavy-tourist" = year-round base is small relative to seasonal load AND winter services meaningfully contract (Cape Cod, Islands, RI south shore, Newport, CT southeast/Mystic, ME southern coast, plus NH Lakes/Whites and VT inland). "summer-surge" = significant seasonal population and seasonal housing stock but an intact year-round town underneath (CT central shoreline, MA South Coast, NH Seacoast, ME interior lakes). "year-round" = genuine commuter/employment towns.
- erosion_note: separated deliberately from surge, because they diverge. Long Island Sound and Narragansett Bay have severe surge and negligible chronic erosion; the RI south shore, outer Cape and Nantucket have both; Casco Bay has neither in the classic sense but has fast-rising inundation frequency. A screen that conflates the two will misprice CT and RI East Bay in opposite directions.

Deliberate methodological calls a reviewer should know about.
1. Parcel over town. Three subregions (MA North Shore, MA South Shore, CT Fairfield shore) are internally bimodal to the point that a town-level score is actively misleading - Cohasset upland and Humarock are the same town-tier and not remotely the same risk. Every one of those notes says so.
2. FEMA zone is a floor, not an answer. Flagged hard for Maine, where the newly revised Cumberland/York FIRMs explicitly do not incorporate sea-level rise or extreme-rainfall trends, and for the inland subregions, where 1 in 3 NFIP claims from 2013-2023 came from outside mapped high-risk zones.
3. Barriers protect less than buyers assume. Two specific corrections are embedded: the Fox Point Hurricane Barrier covers ~280 acres of downtown Providence and nothing in the East Bay, and the New Bedford Hurricane Barrier covers the inner harbor and not Fairhaven/Mattapoisett/Marion/Wareham.
4. Inland is not free. VT/western NE and the CT interior carry genuine fluvial risk (2023/2024 VT floods; August 2024 CT flash flooding with a major disaster declaration for three counties) with worse insurance AVAILABILITY for flood than the coast has for wind. Scoring inland as "no hazard" is the most likely failure mode of a coastal-only screen.

Data currency. Insurance-market figures are 2024-2026 (MPIUA 2024 policy count and 2025 underwriting changes; Maine Bureau of Insurance 2024/2025 approved-rate figures; RIJRA growth reported 2025-26; CT market conditions reported 2025-26). Erosion rates are the published long-term averages, not single-storm events. Population and rail figures are 2024-2026. Numbers I could not verify to a primary source are hedged with "roughly"/"about" in the text; conversely, exact figures (562,843; 430,442; 232,570; 4,941,632; 246,600; 88,509; 29,419) come straight from the cited sources.

Known limitations. (a) I could not reach Census, Wikipedia or MBTA/Amtrak timetables directly - WebFetch returned 403 on all of them - so metro populations and several rail run-times are from secondary aggregators and are cross-checked where possible but should be re-verified against data.census.gov and the operator PDFs before shipping. New Haven MSA in particular has two conflicting figures in circulation (~577k vs ~604k) depending on the CBSA vintage used. (b) Rail times marked "roughly" (Framingham, Worcester, Lowell, Haverhill, individual Metro-North intermediate stations) are interpolated from line end-to-end times and should be pulled from the operator timetables for production. (c) Hurricane-deductible percentages are typical ranges, not a filed rate table; actual deductibles are per-carrier and per-policy.
_meta.anchors_and_rail:
WHY CALIFORNIA'S GATE BREAKS HERE

The California screen used "any city >= 300,000 population." Run that against New England and it returns exactly ONE city: Boston (~650-675k). Every other regional job center falls under the bar - Worcester ~207k (and it is the SECOND-largest city in New England), Providence ~190k, Springfield ~155k, Bridgeport ~148k, Stamford ~137k, New Haven ~135k, Hartford ~121k, Manchester NH ~115k, Portland ME ~68k. New England's municipal boundaries were frozen in the 17th-19th centuries and never annexed their suburbs, so city population is close to meaningless as an employment-market proxy. Hartford is a 121k city inside a 1.02M metro. Portland is a 68k city inside a 563k metro. USE METRO (MSA) POPULATION, NOT CITY POPULATION. That single substitution fixes most of the failure.

===============================================================
A. THE ANCHOR LIST (MSA populations, 2024 Census vintage unless noted)

TIER 1 - metro >= 900k. Primary anchors.
- Boston-Cambridge-Newton MA-NH ....... 4,941,632 (2024); ~10th-11th nationally. The Boston-Worcester-Providence MA-RI-NH-CT CSA is 8,493,824 (2024). Boston recorded the highest year-over-year growth of any major Northeast or Midwest metro in 2023-24 (+1.2%).
- Providence-Warwick RI-MA ............ ~1.21M (2024), ~1.217M (2025)
- Hartford CT ......................... ~1.02M (2024), ~1.03M (2025)
- Bridgeport-Stamford-Danbury CT ...... ~967,000-972,700 (2024); 58th nationally; coextensive with Fairfield County
- NEW YORK-Newark-Jersey City ......... ~19.9M - NOT a New England metro, but the controlling anchor for southwestern Connecticut via Metro-North. Any gate that only measures drive time will (correctly) fail Manhattan from Greenwich and thereby (incorrectly) fail Greenwich. This is the single biggest reason the gate needs a rail branch.

TIER 2 - metro 400k-900k. Real standalone anchors.
- Worcester MA-CT ..................... ~567,000 (2024)
- New Haven CT ........................ ~577,000 (2024) per Census; some aggregators report ~604k on a different CBSA vintage - reconcile before shipping
- Portland-South Portland ME .......... 562,843 (2024)
- Manchester-Nashua NH ................ 430,442 (2024)

TIER 3 - sub-anchors, metro < 400k, but genuine employment nodes that keep a town from being a dead end.
- Springfield MA (~0.69M, verify), Barnstable Town MA 232,570 (2024) - the Cape's own employment center, Norwich-New London CT (~0.27M: Electric Boat, Pfizer Groton, Naval Sub Base, Foxwoods/Mohegan Sun), Portsmouth NH (Pease Tradeport; not its own MSA), New Bedford/Fall River MA, Burlington VT (~0.23M), Bangor ME.

RECOMMENDED THRESHOLD: metro >= 400,000. That yields eight New England anchors (Boston, Providence, Hartford, Bridgeport-Stamford, Worcester, New Haven, Portland, Manchester-Nashua) plus NYC as a rail-only anchor. Dropping to >= 300k adds Springfield and little else; raising to >= 1M collapses you to four and re-creates the California problem.

===============================================================
B. THE COMMUTER RAIL REALITY

--- MBTA COMMUTER RAIL (12 lines, 7-day service; every train terminates at Boston North Station or South Station) ---

NORTH STATION lines:
- Newburyport/Rockport: Chelsea, Lynn, Swampscott, SALEM (~30 min, MBTA's own figure), Beverly, then splits. Rockport branch: Manchester-by-the-Sea, Gloucester, Rockport. Newburyport branch: Hamilton/Wenham, Ipswich, Rowley, Newburyport. Both terminals ~71-77 min end to end.
- Haverhill: Malden, Reading, Andover, Lawrence, Haverhill (~55-60 min).
- Lowell: Winchester, Woburn/Anderson RTC, Wilmington, Lowell (~45 min).
- Fitchburg: Waltham, Lincoln, Concord, W. Concord, Acton, Littleton, Ayer, Shirley, Fitchburg/Wachusett.

SOUTH STATION lines:
- Providence/Stoughton (Northeast Corridor): Hyde Park, Route 128, Canton Jct, Sharon, Mansfield, Attleboro, S. Attleboro, PROVIDENCE (~60-70 min local, faster on express), TF Green Airport (+15 min from Providence), Wickford Junction (+30 min from Providence; ~104 min total to South Station, and NO weekend service Providence-Wickford Jct). Stoughton branch splits at Canton Jct.
- Fall River/New Bedford (SOUTH COAST RAIL) - the biggest change to New England commute geography in a generation. Opened 24 MARCH 2025, first passenger rail to Fall River and New Bedford in 65 years. New stations: Middleborough, East Taunton, Freetown, Church Street, Fall River Depot, New Bedford. ~90 min to South Station; weekday trains every ~70 min, weekends every 2 hours; $12.25 one-way. Any gate built on pre-2025 data scores this whole region as unreachable and is simply wrong.
- Kingston: Braintree, S. Weymouth, Abington, Whitman, Hanson, Halifax, Kingston (~61 min); Plymouth branch is limited.
- Greenbush: Braintree, Weymouth Landing, E. Weymouth, W. Hingham, Nantasket Jct, Cohasset, N. Scituate, Greenbush (~57-59 min end to end). This is how the MA South Shore gets a real commute.
- Framingham/Worcester: Newton stops, Wellesley, Natick, FRAMINGHAM (~40-50 min), Ashland, Southborough, Westborough, Grafton, WORCESTER (~80-90 min). MBTA's "30-30" program targets all-day 30-min bidirectional zonal express to Worcester + 30-min local to Framingham.
- Franklin/Foxboro, Needham, Fairmount. Fairmount is entirely inside Boston, runs 30-min all-day headways as of 1 Dec 2025, and has grown from 789 daily riders (2012) to 4,402 (2024) - more than double pre-pandemic. Battery-electric conversion slipped to ~2030, then 20-min headways.

--- METRO-NORTH NEW HAVEN LINE (MTA) - the NYC anchor ---
Grand Central to: Greenwich, Cos Cob, Riverside, Old Greenwich, STAMFORD, Noroton Heights, Darien, Rowayton, South Norwalk, East Norwalk, Westport, Green's Farms, Southport, FAIRFIELD, Fairfield Metro, BRIDGEPORT, Stratford, Milford, West Haven, NEW HAVEN.
Times: Stamford-GCT ~41 min fastest / ~50 min typical express / ~58 min average / up to 1h15 local. Greenwich ~45-55. Darien/Rowayton/S. Norwalk ~55-65. Westport ~60-70. Fairfield ~65-75. Bridgeport ~70-80. New Haven-GCT currently 98 min to over 2 hours on locals; under the 29 March 2026 schedule (rev. 7/13/26) SIX trains now run New Haven-GCT in 90 minutes or less, after signal upgrades cut roughly 10 minutes. Peak: arrivals GCT 6-10am, departures 4-8pm.
Branches (New Canaan, Danbury, Waterbury) require a transfer at Stamford/S. Norwalk/Bridgeport and are materially slower - do not score them as main-line.

--- CTrail SHORE LINE EAST - real, but thin ---
New Haven State St and Union Station to Branford, Guilford, Madison, Clinton, Westbrook, Old Saybrook, New London. Seven days a week including holidays. Limited weekday through-service to Stamford on select trains. Old Saybrook-New Haven roughly 45 min; New London-New Haven roughly 60-65 min.
THE CAVEAT THAT MATTERS: 246,600 total riders in 2025 and only ~900 average weekday riders in Q4 2025. That is a skeletal service. It is a genuine amenity for a hybrid worker and NOT a substitute for a car. Amtrak Northeast Regional also stops at Old Saybrook and New London (faster, much pricier).

--- CTrail HARTFORD LINE ---
New Haven - Wallingford - Meriden - Berlin - Hartford - Windsor - Windsor Locks - Springfield MA. ~81 min New Haven to Springfield. ~18 weekday round trips (CTrail + Amtrak combined), 12-13 weekend. ~2,000 average weekday riders; 750,000+ annual riders in 2024. This is what makes Meriden, Berlin, Wallingford and Windsor commutable to either New Haven or Hartford.

--- AMTRAK DOWNEASTER (NNEPRA) ---
Brunswick - Freeport - PORTLAND - Old Orchard Beach (seasonal) - Saco - Wells - DOVER NH - Durham NH - EXETER NH - Haverhill MA - Woburn/Anderson RTC - Boston North Station.
Five daily round trips. ~3h25 end to end; Boston-Portland ~2h35 (e.g. 8:50am departure, 11:25am arrival). Exeter-North Station ~70 min. Fares $3-$36 value, $5-$38 flex.
BE HONEST ABOUT WHAT THIS IS: an intercity train with a handful of commuter-usable slots at Exeter/Durham/Dover/Haverhill, not a turn-up-and-go railroad. Five round trips means missing one train costs you hours. Score it as a partial-week/hybrid enabler, never as a daily commute.

--- AMTRAK NORTHEAST CORRIDOR (worth flagging) ---
Providence-Boston in ~35-45 min on Regional/Acela versus ~60-70 on the MBTA, at roughly 3-5x the fare. A Providence or East Bay buyer has a fast-but-expensive option the MBTA timetable alone does not show.

===============================================================
C. WHICH TOWNS ACTUALLY GET A GENUINE RAIL COMMUTE

To BOSTON (station within ~10 min drive, <= ~75 min scheduled peak run):
North Shore - Swampscott, Salem, Beverly, Hamilton/Wenham, Ipswich, Rowley, Newburyport, Manchester-by-the-Sea, Gloucester, Rockport.
North/Northwest - Winchester, Woburn, Wilmington, Lowell, Reading, Wakefield, Andover, Haverhill, Concord, Acton, Littleton, Waltham, Lincoln.
West - Wellesley, Natick, Framingham, Ashland, Southborough, Westborough, Grafton (Worcester itself at ~80-90 min is a stretch but defensible).
Southwest - Needham, Dedham, Norwood, Walpole, Franklin, Foxboro.
South - Braintree, Weymouth, Hingham, Cohasset, Scituate (Greenbush ~57 min), Abington, Whitman, Hanson, Halifax, Kingston (~61 min). Plus commuter BOAT from Hingham and Hull.
Southeast - Sharon, Mansfield, Attleboro, S. Attleboro, Providence RI, Warwick/TF Green.
NEW since March 2025 - Taunton (East Taunton), Freetown, Fall River, New Bedford (~90 min).

To NEW YORK via Metro-North (this is where the NYC anchor pays off):
Solid 5-day commute - Greenwich, Cos Cob, Riverside, Old Greenwich, Stamford, Noroton Heights, Darien, Rowayton, South Norwalk, East Norwalk, Westport, Green's Farms, Southport, Fairfield, Fairfield Metro, Bridgeport.
Hybrid only (80-120 min) - Stratford, Milford, West Haven, New Haven.
Score DOWN, not up - New Canaan, Wilton, Redding, Bethel, Danbury and the whole Waterbury branch: transfer-dependent and slow.

To NEW HAVEN or HARTFORD by rail:
Shore Line East - Branford, Guilford, Madison, Clinton, Westbrook, Old Saybrook (to New Haven).
Hartford Line - Wallingford, Meriden, Berlin, Windsor, Windsor Locks, Springfield.

NOT RAIL-SERVED AT ALL (drive-only). A rail-ONLY gate would wrongly kill these; a drive-only gate would wrongly kill the list above. You need both branches.
- All of Cape Cod (CapeFLYER is Fri-Sun summer only), Martha's Vineyard, Nantucket
- The entire RI East Bay: Barrington, Warren, Bristol, Tiverton, Little Compton - the Providence Line runs down the WEST side of the Bay
- Newport / Aquidneck Island (bridge- and toll-dependent)
- RI south shore: Westerly, Charlestown, South Kingstown, Narragansett - only the Wickford Junction park-and-ride, ~104 min
- The NH Seacoast proper: Portsmouth, Rye, New Castle, Greenland, Hampton, North Hampton. Nearest rail is the Downeaster at Exeter/Dover, or driving to Newburyport MA for the MBTA.
- Manchester and Nashua NH - no passenger rail to Boston exists; the proposed Capitol Corridor extension remains unfunded
- Southern Maine off the Downeaster stops: Kittery, York, Ogunquit, Cape Elizabeth, Kennebunkport
- MA South Coast towns off the new line: Westport, Dartmouth, Mattapoisett, Marion, Wareham

===============================================================
D. RECOMMENDED GATE DESIGN

1. Replace ">= 300k city" with: within 60 minutes DRIVE **OR** 75 minutes SCHEDULED PEAK RAIL of a Tier-1 or Tier-2 anchor (metro >= 400k). Either branch passes.
2. Add NYC as a rail-only anchor reachable from the Metro-North New Haven Line main line. Drive time to Manhattan correctly fails; rail time correctly passes. Without this special case the screen throws away the highest-income commuter belt in New England.
3. Make rail a BONUS with a service-quality floor, not a binary "has a station." Require a station within ~10 min drive AND >= 8 weekday peak trains AND <= 75 min scheduled run. This is what separates Salem (30 min, frequent) from an Old Saybrook Shore Line East platform (~900 weekday riders system-wide) or a Wells Downeaster stop (5 round trips a day). Encode the frequency, or the model will treat those as equivalent and they are not.
4. Penalize choke-point access explicitly, because drive time alone hides it: the Sagamore and Bourne bridges are the only two roads onto Cape Cod with in-season volume up 59% and 49% and both are slated for replacement; Aquidneck Island is reached only by tolled bridges; southern NH commuters funnel through I-93 and Route 3 with no rail alternative at all.
5. Refresh the rail layer at least annually. South Coast Rail (March 2025) added four towns and the Metro-North March 2026 schedule cut roughly 10 minutes off New Haven runs. A gate built on 2023 timetables is already wrong in two places.
_meta.town_crosswalk: hazard subregions inherit town lists from the climate layer via an explicit crosswalk; unmapped hazard subregions (islands, Newport/Aquidneck, far interior) carry no towns and simply contribute no hazard opinion

CT Fairfield shore.fema_note: FEMA maps for Greenwich, Westport, Fairfield, Stratford and Milford are dense with Zone VE (wave action) and Zone AE along Long Island Sound; recent map revisions have moved parcels INTO higher-risk zones, not out. CT's 2022 State Building Code incorporates ASCE 24-21 flood-resistant design, so a substantial improvement on a pre-FIRM beach house triggers full elevation compliance. Zone flips street-by-street: VE frontage often drops to AE one row back and to X two rows back.
CT Fairfield shore.wind_deductible: Named-storm/hurricane percentage deductible is standard on shore policies, typically 1-5% of Coverage A (not a flat dollar amount). CT is one of 19 states plus DC that permit them. Trigger is the National Hurricane Center naming the storm, NOT a wind-speed threshold - so a weak named tropical storm can trigger a $40k deductible on an $800k dwelling while a 70 mph unnamed nor'easter triggers only the flat $1k.
CT Fairfield shore.erosion_note: Long Island Sound is fetch-limited, so chronic shoreline retreat is modest compared with the open Atlantic. The real hazard is surge amplification: the western Sound funnels and piles water for a hurricane tracking to its west, which is the single worst surge geometry in Connecticut. Erosion is not the screen here - inundation elevation is.
CT Fairfield shore.note: Worst risk/price combination in New England: highest-value housing stock + genuine VE exposure + Metro-North premium already capitalized into price. Screen at the PARCEL level, not the town level - Greenwich backcountry and Westport north of the Post Road are effectively hazard-free while Fairfield Beach Road and Lordship are not. Coastal Fairfield/New Haven/New London county homeowners are in the hardest CT market in years; carriers are issuing steep increases and non-renewals on homes with zero loss history, and wood-shake roofs near the water quote 3-5x an equivalent inland home.

CT central shoreline.fema_note: Branford through Old Lyme: extensive AE with VE on the beach colonies and barrier spits. Milford, Stratford and Old Saybrook are documented repetitive tidal-flooding towns - surge and even routine spring tides fill streets and ground-floor garages, corrode utilities and undermine foundations. Clinton, Old Saybrook and Waterford have already adopted local elevation/freeboard standards ABOVE the FEMA minimum for new or substantially improved structures; several shoreline towns participate in the Community Rating System, which discounts NFIP premiums. Statewide CT has recorded 29,419 NFIP claims since 1978 totaling ~$544.9M.
CT central shoreline.wind_deductible: Same 1-5% named-storm deductible regime as Fairfield County. Expect a percentage wind deductible on anything within roughly a mile of the water; expect it to be non-negotiable on VE parcels.
CT central shoreline.erosion_note: Low chronic retreat (fetch-limited Sound), but marsh drowning and increasing tidal-inundation frequency of access roads is the live problem. A house that is dry can still be cut off - screen the ROAD elevation, not just the pad elevation.
CT central shoreline.note: A large share of the shoreline housing stock here is converted seasonal cottage - Point O'Woods (Old Lyme), Grove Beach (Westbrook), Indian Neck (Branford) - built on slab at grade in the 1920s-50s and never engineered for the current code. Guilford, Madison and Branford village centers are genuine year-round towns. This is the best rail-served coastal value in New England on paper (Shore Line East), but SLE is thin: ~246,600 total riders in 2025 and only ~900 average weekday riders in Q4 2025. Do not underwrite a purchase on SLE alone.

CT southeast shore (New London / Mystic.fema_note: AE/VE around the Thames and Mystic River mouths, Napatree/Watch Hill approach, and the Groton/Noank necks. Mystic borough's historic waterfront stock sits at or barely above BFE. Waterford has adopted above-minimum elevation standards.
CT southeast shore (New London / Mystic.wind_deductible: 1-5% named-storm deductible standard on waterfront; this is the most hurricane-exposed stretch of the CT coast because it faces the open approach rather than the sheltered western Sound.
CT southeast shore (New London / Mystic.erosion_note: Mostly armored or bedrock; Napatree and the Stonington barrier features are the mobile exceptions. The 1938 hurricane rewrote this shoreline and remains the design event.
CT southeast shore (New London / Mystic.note: Job anchor is Norwich-New London (roughly 0.27M metro, small): Electric Boat/General Dynamics, Pfizer Groton, Naval Submarine Base, Mohegan Sun and Foxwoods. That's a real but narrow employment base - single-employer exposure is a legitimate underwriting concern here in a way it is not in Boston or Hartford. Served by Shore Line East and by Amtrak Northeast Regional at New London and Old Saybrook.

RI East Bay.fema_note: Barrington, Warren, Bristol, Tiverton: extensive AE along the Palmer River, Warren River, Hundred Acre Cove and Bristol Harbor. CRITICAL and widely misunderstood - the Fox Point Hurricane Barrier protects roughly 280 acres of DOWNTOWN PROVIDENCE ONLY. It does nothing for East Bay towns. Upper Narragansett Bay is a surge funnel: the 1938 hurricane is the design event, Sandy pushed 7.6 ft above mean sea level into the Bay in 2012, and the Fox Point barrier itself is only rated to ~22 ft of surge (roughly a Category 3).
RI East Bay.wind_deductible: Rhode Island statute caps the hurricane deductible on homeowners policies at 5% of the insured value (RIGL 27-76); 1-5% is the normal range and waterfront lands at or near the cap.
RI East Bay.erosion_note: Minimal open-ocean erosion - bay shoreline is low bluff or already armored. The hazard here is inundation depth, not shoreline retreat. Do not let a clean erosion picture read as a clean hazard picture.
RI East Bay.note: The RI 'good schools + Providence commute' pocket (Barrington especially). No commuter rail whatsoever - the MBTA Providence/Stoughton Line runs down the WEST side of the Bay, so East Bay towns are 100% drive-and-bridge dependent. RIJRA (the RI FAIR Plan) has added ~2,000 policies in two years and roughly 50% of its book now sits in coastal territories; most new policies within 3 miles of the RI coast are either materially more expensive than inland or simply unavailable in the voluntary market.

RI south shore.fema_note: Westerly/Misquamicut, Charlestown, South Kingstown/Matunuck and Narragansett are classic barrier-beach VE frontage backed by AE around the coastal salt ponds. This is the most directly hurricane-exposed shoreline in southern New England - it faces open ocean with no Cape Cod or Long Island in front of it. Sandy devastated Misquamicut, Matunuck, Charlestown and Narragansett in 2012.
RI south shore.wind_deductible: 5% statutory cap (RIGL 27-76); oceanfront routinely quotes at or near the cap. On a $900k dwelling that is a $45,000 first-dollar exposure per named storm.
RI south shore.erosion_note: HIGHEST chronic erosion in southern New England. Measured retreat runs up to ~1.15 m/yr (~3.8 ft/yr) in places. At Matunuck the beach is down to roughly 12 ft wide at high tide in spots. RI CRMC publishes regulatory shoreline-change maps from Watch Hill to Narragansett Pier - USE THEM, they are the legal basis for setback and rebuild decisions. Projections have the current rate roughly doubling by 2100 (2.5x by 2065 on the high case), which would put Matunuck at 9-12 ft/yr.
RI south shore.note: The single strongest 'do not buy the front row' subregion in the whole screen. Erosion here is not a slow amenity discount, it is a finite countdown on the parcel. No commuter rail; the nearest MBTA station is Wickford Junction (~104 min to Boston South Station, and no weekend service between Providence and Wickford Junction). Rhode Island drew a record 29.4M visitors in 2024 spending $6B, and tourism supports 88,509 jobs = ~13% of state employment - which is exactly why the beach towns are seasonal.

RI Newport / Aquidneck.fema_note: AE/VE around Newport Harbor, the Point, Easton's Beach/Middletown, Third Beach and the Portsmouth shoreline. Much of Newport's historic colonial stock is at low elevation on fill near the harbor and is effectively unelevatable without destroying the asset.
RI Newport / Aquidneck.wind_deductible: 1-5% named-storm, 5% statutory cap. Historic-district construction costs push replacement-cost valuations high, which inflates the dollar deductible even at a modest percentage.
RI Newport / Aquidneck.erosion_note: Rocky and armored on the Ocean Drive/Cliff Walk side (Cliff Walk itself has repeated collapse and closure events); the sand-beach exceptions are Easton's and Sachuest/Second Beach.
RI Newport / Aquidneck.note: Bridge-dependent and toll-dependent (Pell/Newport Bridge, Mount Hope Bridge, Sakonnet River Bridge) with no rail at all. Economy is Navy (NAVSTA Newport/Naval War College) plus a heavy seasonal tourism overlay - Newport has been a resort economy since the Gilded Age and its year-round base is small relative to its summer load. Screen for winter services, not August charm.

MA Cape Cod.fema_note: Extensive AE and VE around every harbor and along both the bayside and soundside. As of 2025 the FAIR Plan requires any NEW policy on a property inside a Special Flood Hazard Area in a Massachusetts CZM community to ALSO carry a separate flood policy - so on the Cape, 'flood insurance optional' is increasingly false even when the lender does not force it.
MA Cape Cod.wind_deductible: 1-5% of Coverage A named-storm deductible is standard, expressed as a percentage of the dwelling limit. On an $800k dwelling a 5% deductible is $40,000 out of pocket before the policy pays anything for storm damage. Note the counterintuitive local fact: on the Cape the FAIR Plan is often the CHEAPEST policy you can actually buy, not the most expensive - the voluntary market has largely left.
MA Cape Cod.erosion_note: Outer Cape (Eastham through Truro) oceanfront averages about 3 ft/yr; historical Wellfleet/Truro segments have run as high as ~9 ft/yr and Chatham's North Beach barrier has ranged from ~3 to ~19 ft/yr. Nine Chatham homes have been lost to the sea in recent years. Truro and Wellfleet clifftop houses are physically lifted and moved inland most summers. Sandwich required an ~$8.95M nourishment project (300,000+ cubic yards piped from Scusset Beach) after the Army Corps found the threat to Town Neck had reached 'critical mass'.
MA Cape Cod.note: The clearest insurance-market crisis in New England. The Massachusetts FAIR Plan (MPIUA) is now the LARGEST insurer on Cape Cod and the Islands: roughly 4 in 10 homes on the Cape and Islands are on the plan, up from ~33% in 2023. MPIUA insured 173,000+ properties in 2024 - its first single-year policy-count increase since 2017 and its largest one-year jump in about two decades. Since 2/1/2025 new business requires Coverage A at >=90% of estimated reconstruction cost (up from 80%), which mechanically raises both premium and the dollar value of any percentage deductible. FAIR Plan premiums typically run 15-30% above standard-market rates with none of the usual discounts. NO commuter rail (CapeFLYER is summer Friday-Sunday only) and the Sagamore and Bourne bridges are a genuine single point of failure with in-season volumes up 59% and 49% respectively - and both are slated for replacement, so price in years of construction disruption.

MA Islands (Nantucket / Martha's Vineyar.fema_note: AE/VE around Nantucket town/Brant Point, Madaket, Edgartown and Oak Bluffs harbors. Nantucket maintains its own FEMA Coastal Erosion Hazard Map layer in addition to the FIRMs - a signal that the FIRM alone understates the risk here.
MA Islands (Nantucket / Martha's Vineyar.wind_deductible: 1-5% named-storm on multi-million-dollar dwelling limits - a 5% deductible on a $3M dwelling is a $150,000 first-dollar exposure. Island rates remain very high, though 2025-26 quotes came in somewhat improved versus the prior season.
MA Islands (Nantucket / Martha's Vineyar.erosion_note: The most aggressive erosion story in New England. 'Sconset Bluff's geotube was called 'almost a complete failure' by the Nantucket Conservation Commission chair in March 2025 after splitting open in winter storms; 27 homes along Baxter Road have already been relocated. Nantucket's south shore erodes ~2.2 ft/yr, has retreated a half mile since colonial times, and the eastern shore has lost roughly 100 ft in the last decade. Private sand-hauling to armor individual lots is now depleting the neighborhoods that supply the sand.
MA Islands (Nantucket / Martha's Vineyar.note: Ferry/air dependent, extreme seasonality, extreme insurance stress, active managed-retreat policy discussion. Include in the screen only as an explicit exclusion or a deliberate second-home category - it should never pass a primary-residence quality gate.

MA South Coast.fema_note: AE/VE all along Buzzards Bay - Westport Point, Padanaram, Clarks Cove, Fairhaven, Mattapoisett/Marion necks, Onset and Wareham. The New Bedford Hurricane Barrier protects the INNER HARBOR ONLY; Fairhaven, Mattapoisett, Marion and Wareham are outside it.
MA South Coast.wind_deductible: 1-5% named-storm deductible; coastal Bristol and Plymouth County ZIPs are routinely assigned to MPIUA. Wareham/Mattapoisett/Marion waterfront frequently cannot place voluntary-market wind at all.
MA South Coast.erosion_note: Moderate and fetch-limited - the bayside shoreline does not retreat the way the outer Cape does. The hazard is surge INUNDATION of the low necks and causeways, not chronic loss of land.
MA South Coast.note: Buzzards Bay is the worst hurricane surge funnel in New England - a southeast-facing V that concentrates water at its head. The 1938 hurricane, Carol (1954) and Bob (1991) all did their signature damage here. This is also the subregion whose commute math CHANGED: South Coast Rail opened 24 March 2025, the first passenger rail to Fall River and New Bedford in 65 years - roughly 90 minutes to Boston South Station, weekday trains about every 70 minutes, weekends every 2 hours, $12.25 one-way, via new stations at Middleborough, East Taunton, Freetown, Church Street, Fall River Depot and New Bedford. A drive-time-only gate scored this region as unreachable in 2024 and is simply wrong in 2026. Note the rail benefit is town-specific: Westport, Dartmouth, Mattapoisett, Marion and Wareham are NOT on the new line.

MA South Shore.fema_note: Among the most documented repetitive-loss coastlines in the country. Scituate and its residents/businesses have drawn ~$60M from the NFIP since the 1970s; some Scituate properties have taken 8 or more flood payments and one has flooded 14 times. Marshfield has 19 SEVERE repetitive loss properties. The most exposed pockets are the coastal barriers: Humarock (Scituate), Brant Rock (Marshfield) and North Duxbury Beach. Scituate runs an active FEMA-grant home-elevation program - a strong signal the town knows its own stock is under-elevated.
MA South Shore.wind_deductible: 1-5% named-storm deductible standard. Cape Cod, the Islands and the South Shore pay the highest homeowners premiums in Massachusetts. Placement often turns on the condition and ownership of the adjacent SEAWALL - a privately-owned seawall in poor repair is an underwriting decline, and repair liability can fall on the homeowner.
MA South Shore.erosion_note: Seawall-dependent, and the governing hazard here is NOR'EASTERS, not hurricanes. The Blizzard of 1978 destroyed 300+ Scituate homes; the No-Name Storm of 1991 destroyed roughly 100 more; the January and March 2018 nor'easters put the National Guard into these streets. Protecting the exposed Massachusetts coastal barriers with dunes, seawalls and selective buyouts has been estimated at more than $500M over 50 years - and a buyout conversation is already live for the worst repetitive-loss parcels.
MA South Shore.note: Important nuance: the town-level and parcel-level pictures diverge more here than anywhere else. Hingham, Cohasset and Duxbury upland are excellent, low-hazard, rail-served commuter towns; Humarock and Brant Rock a mile away are among the highest-risk residential parcels in the state. Genuinely rail-served: Greenbush Line (Hingham/Cohasset/Scituate) runs about 57-59 minutes end-to-end to South Station, and the Kingston Line runs about 61 minutes - plus commuter boat service from Hingham and Hull.

MA North Shore.fema_note: Sharply bimodal. High AE/VE exposure on the barrier and low-lying frontage: Revere Beach, Winthrop, Lynn Shore, Plum Island (Newbury/Newburyport) and Salisbury Beach. But the Cape Ann bedrock coast - Marblehead, Manchester-by-the-Sea, Gloucester, Rockport - sits on ledge and has comparatively little SFHA residential exposure. Rate this subregion at the parcel, not the town.
MA North Shore.wind_deductible: Named-storm percentage deductibles are common on true beachfront and frequently absent one or two streets inland. This is the coastal Massachusetts subregion where a modest change of address most reliably removes the percentage deductible entirely.
MA North Shore.erosion_note: Plum Island is the state's most publicized erosion crisis - homes have been lost and a state report recommended adopting no-construction buffer zones and experimenting with new mitigation approaches. Salisbury Beach has had repeated privately-funded nourishment wash out within months. By contrast the Cape Ann granite headlands are effectively stable on any horizon that matters to a mortgage.
MA North Shore.note: The best coastal + rail combination in New England, and the one place where you can get salt water and a real Boston commute without buying a hazard. Newburyport/Rockport Line: Salem is about 30 minutes to North Station (MBTA's own figure), and the Newburyport and Rockport terminals run roughly 71-77 minutes. Rule: buy bedrock, not barrier beach. Marblehead, Manchester-by-the-Sea, Beverly, Salem and Rockport pass; Plum Island, Salisbury Beach and Winthrop/Revere oceanfront should be flagged.

NH Seacoast.fema_note: VE along the wave-exposed Route 1A beach frontage with AE across the Hampton beach village and its back marsh. FEMA estimates over 9% of parcels in Rockingham County fall inside SFHAs. The alarming statistic: Hampton alone accounts for 24% of ALL National Flood Insurance Program policies in New Hampshire and 11% of all NH repetitive-loss properties - yet the town has only about 85 active flood policies, meaning hundreds of owners in the flood-prone core are underinsured or entirely uninsured. Do not treat 'the seller has no flood policy' as evidence of no flood risk here.
NH Seacoast.wind_deductible: New Hampshire does NOT have a statutory hurricane-deductible program the way MA, RI and CT do. Percentage wind deductibles here are carrier-imposed on oceanfront risk rather than mandated, so they vary a lot by carrier and are more negotiable than in southern New England. Verify per-quote rather than assuming.
NH Seacoast.erosion_note: The Route 1A shore is largely armored, so chronic retreat is suppressed. The more useful signal is high-tide/nuisance flooding frequency, which is already measurable at the Hampton tide gauge and rises steeply with the projected 1-2 ft of additional sea-level rise by 2060. Seabrook has a completed municipal vulnerability assessment worth reading before buying there.
NH Seacoast.note: No MBTA commuter rail reaches New Hampshire at all. The Amtrak Downeaster stops at Exeter, Durham and Dover - Exeter to North Station is roughly 70 minutes - but Portsmouth itself has NO station. Driving Portsmouth to Boston is ~57 miles / ~67 minutes free-flow and materially worse at peak. Many seacoast commuters instead drive to Newburyport MA and take the MBTA. The genuine draw is fiscal: no state income tax and no sales tax, which is a real and permanent carry advantage over MA/RI/CT.

ME Casco Bay.fema_note: AE around Portland's working waterfront, Back Cove, the Fore River and the Scarborough marsh. Revised FEMA maps for Cumberland and York counties have been released - but the critical caveat is that the new maps are NOT drawn for a changing climate: they do not account for sea-level rise or extreme-rainfall trends. Treat the FEMA zone here as a floor, not an answer, and layer a sea-level-rise viewer on top of it.
ME Casco Bay.wind_deductible: Maine is not a statutory hurricane-deductible state. Percentage wind deductibles appear carrier-by-carrier on true oceanfront and island property; most inland-of-the-shore Casco Bay homes carry an ordinary flat deductible.
ME Casco Bay.erosion_note: Sea level around Maine is now rising as fast as roughly 1 inch every 6 years, and tidal flooding in some areas is up 183% since 2000. One additional foot of rise implies roughly 8x more frequent coastal flooding - on the order of 60 flood days per year. Rocky/ledge shoreline means little classic erosion; the mechanism here is progressive inundation and drainage failure.
ME Casco Bay.note: Portland is a genuine year-round metro (Portland-South Portland MSA 562,843 in 2024), not a resort - so this is the one Maine coastal subregion with a real local job market rather than a seasonal one. Statewide approved homeowners rate increases averaged 12.8% in 2024 before slowing to about 2.9% in 2025; coastal towns run above the statewide average and the January and March 2024 storm losses are still working through carrier data on a lag. Harpswell, Chebeague and the Casco Bay islands are a separate, much more seasonal and much less serviced category than mainland Falmouth/Yarmouth/Cape Elizabeth.

ME southern coast.fema_note: AE/VE concentrated on the sand-beach frontages and their back-barrier marshes - Old Orchard Beach, Wells, Ogunquit, Higgins Beach and Pine Point in Scarborough, Long Sands/Short Sands in York. Same critical caveat as Casco Bay: the new York County FIRMs are not climate-adjusted.
ME southern coast.wind_deductible: Carrier-imposed percentage wind deductibles on oceanfront; no statutory program. Older un-elevated beach cottages are the hardest placements.
ME southern coast.erosion_note: Maine's sand beaches are a small, sediment-starved fraction of an otherwise rocky coast, and they are heavily seawalled at Old Orchard Beach and Wells. Chronic retreat plus discrete storm-event damage of the January 2024 type is the pattern; there is very little sediment supply to recover with.
ME southern coast.note: The most seasonal subregion in the screen after Cape Cod and the Islands. Kennebunkport's population TRIPLES in summer, Wells nearly QUADRUPLES, Kennebunk rises ~50%, and Ogunquit's daily summer average is estimated at 75,000-80,000 against a tiny year-round base. Old Orchard Beach has 1,000+ short-term rental listings and February occupancy of about 32% - the town genuinely empties. Screen for year-round services: grocery, urgent care, plowed roads, a school district that is not shrinking. Rail is intercity only (Downeaster at Wells, Saco and seasonally Old Orchard Beach); the realistic job anchor is Portsmouth NH or Portland ME, not Boston.

MA MetroWest / I-495 interior.fema_note: Small riverine AE footprints along the Charles, Sudbury, Assabet and Concord Rivers and around wetland systems. Most parcels are Zone X. The residual risk is pluvial (rainfall) flooding of finished basements, which no FEMA map shows and no standard homeowners policy covers.
MA MetroWest / I-495 interior.wind_deductible: None typical - flat dollar deductible ($500-$2,500). No named-storm percentage deductible.
MA MetroWest / I-495 interior.erosion_note: Not applicable. Substitute hazards: ice storms and wind-driven tree failure on mature-canopy lots, and long-duration power outages.
MA MetroWest / I-495 interior.note: The inland control group. Densest commuter-rail coverage in New England - Framingham/Worcester, Fitchburg, Franklin and Needham lines all run through it. Framingham is roughly 40-50 minutes to South Station and the MBTA's '30-30' program targets all-day 30-minute bidirectional zonal-express service to Worcester plus 30-minute local service to Framingham. This is what a coastal town's hazard/insurance load is being paid FOR - quantify the premium against this baseline.

MA Worcester County interior.fema_note: Riverine AE along the Blackstone, Nashua and Quinebaug and around the Quabbin/Wachusett watersheds. Very limited residential SFHA exposure.
MA Worcester County interior.erosion_note: Not applicable. Ice storm and heavy-wet-snow tree damage is the dominant weather loss driver.
MA Worcester County interior.note: Worcester is the second-largest city in New England (city population passed 207,000) and the Worcester MA-CT MSA runs about 567,000 - a legitimate standalone job anchor, not just a Boston suburb. Worcester to South Station is roughly 80-90 minutes by rail. Best price-per-square-foot in eastern Massachusetts with essentially no coastal hazard load and no percentage wind deductible.

MA Merrimack Valley interior.fema_note: Riverine AE along the Merrimack, Shawsheen and Spicket Rivers - a real and locally significant floodplain through Lowell, Lawrence and Haverhill, but a small share of parcels.
MA Merrimack Valley interior.wind_deductible: None typical inland. Note that Amesbury/Salisbury edge toward coastal rating territories.
MA Merrimack Valley interior.note: Rail-strong: Lowell Line (~45 min to North Station) and Haverhill Line (~55-60 min). Also the practical rail catchment for southern New Hampshire residents, who drive south to Lowell, Anderson/Woburn or Haverhill because NH has no MBTA service.

MA Pioneer Valley / Connecticut River.fema_note: Genuine riverine AE along the Connecticut, Westfield, Deerfield and Millers Rivers - the 2011 Irene and 2023 events showed this is not theoretical. Zero coastal exposure.
MA Pioneer Valley / Connecticut River.erosion_note: Not applicable; riverbank and streambank erosion after high-rainfall events.
MA Pioneer Valley / Connecticut River.note: No Boston commute of any kind. Anchors are Springfield MA and Hartford CT, linked by the CTrail Hartford Line (New Haven-Hartford-Springfield, about 81 minutes end to end). Cheapest housing in Massachusetts. The honest hazard trade is coastal surge OUT, freshwater flash flooding IN - and freshwater flooding is uninsured far more often, because 1 in 3 NFIP claims from 2013-2023 came from OUTSIDE mapped high-risk zones.

CT interior (Hartford / Farmington Valle.fema_note: Riverine AE along the Connecticut, Farmington, Housatonic and Naugatuck Rivers. In August 2024 slow-moving thunderstorms dumped as much as 16 inches of rain in 6-8 hours in western Connecticut, sending the Housatonic, Naugatuck and Little Rivers over their banks and producing a FEMA Major Disaster Declaration for Fairfield, New Haven and Litchfield Counties. Much of the worst damage was outside mapped SFHAs.
CT interior (Hartford / Farmington Valle.wind_deductible: None typical - flat dollar deductible. This is the direct contrast to the CT shore, where the same carrier will impose 1-5% of Coverage A.
CT interior (Hartford / Farmington Valle.erosion_note: Not applicable. Streambank erosion and culvert/road washout after convective rainfall is the live inland analogue.
CT interior (Hartford / Farmington Valle.note: Hartford metro is roughly 1.02-1.03M - the third-largest job market in New England (insurance, Pratt & Whitney/RTX, UConn Health, state government). CTrail Hartford Line serves Wallingford, Meriden, Berlin, Hartford, Windsor and Windsor Locks: about 18 weekday round trips, ~2,000 average weekday riders and 750,000+ annual riders in 2024. Thin but genuine. The flash-flood risk here is real and should not be scored as 'no hazard' just because it is not coastal.

RI interior.fema_note: Riverine AE along the Blackstone, Pawtuxet and Woonasquatucket. The March 2010 flood is the local design event and it was freshwater, not coastal.
RI interior.note: This is literally the comparison Rhode Island's own reporting draws: a coastal home will take more wind damage 'than houses in Johnston or Woonsocket', and most new policies within 3 miles of the coast are more expensive or unavailable while inland placement is routine. Cranston, Johnston, Smithfield, Lincoln, Cumberland and North Kingstown inland give Providence-metro access at normal insurance cost. Providence MSA is roughly 1.21M (2024).

NH interior (Manchester-Nashua / Merrima.fema_note: Riverine AE along the Merrimack, Souhegan and Piscataquog. Limited residential exposure.
NH interior (Manchester-Nashua / Merrima.erosion_note: Not applicable. Ice storms and wind-driven tree failure are the loss drivers.
NH interior (Manchester-Nashua / Merrima.note: Manchester-Nashua MSA 430,442 (2024) is a real secondary anchor in its own right (healthcare, defense/advanced manufacturing, BAE Systems, Fidelity in Merrimack). No passenger rail to Boston exists - the long-proposed Capitol Corridor extension remains unfunded - so this is a car-or-bus commute on I-93/Route 3, or drive-to-Lowell/Anderson-Woburn for MBTA. No income or sales tax. The cleanest 'no coastal hazard, no percentage wind deductible, still commutable' quadrant in the screen.

NH Lakes Region / White Mountains interi.fema_note: Lakeshore and riverine AE (Winnipesaukee, Pemigewasset, Saco headwaters). No coastal exposure at all.
NH Lakes Region / White Mountains interi.erosion_note: Not applicable. Winter loads - ice dams, roof snow load, tree failure - dominate.
NH Lakes Region / White Mountains interi.note: Included as the inland proof that seasonality is NOT a coastal-only problem. Wolfeboro, Meredith, North Conway and the ski towns have summer-and-winter tourist economies with thin shoulder seasons, seasonal service closures and a short-term-rental-driven housing market. No commute to any Tier-1 or Tier-2 anchor - exclude from any primary-residence gate on access grounds, not hazard grounds.

ME interior (Lakes Region / inland Cumbe.fema_note: Lakeshore and riverine AE (Sebago, Saco, Presumpscot, Androscoggin). No coastal exposure.
ME interior (Lakes Region / inland Cumbe.note: Gorham, Windham, Standish, Buxton, Gray and New Gloucester give 20-40 minute access to Portland's 562,843-person metro at normal insurance cost and with none of the coastal FIRM/wind-deductible load. This is the highest-value inland alternative in Maine and the correct comparison set for anyone considering ME southern coast.

VT and western New England interior.fema_note: Zero coastal exposure but SERIOUS riverine risk. Vermont's Winooski, Mad, White and Lamoille valleys, Otter Creek and the Connecticut River border flooded catastrophically in July 2023 and again in summer 2024, hitting many of the same communities still recovering. Many of the hardest-hit homes sat well outside any FEMA high-risk zone.
VT and western New England interior.erosion_note: Not applicable coastally. Fluvial erosion - rivers cutting new channels through valley-floor property - is the Vermont-specific mechanism and it destroys parcels outright, much like coastal erosion does.
VT and western New England interior.note: Included as the honest counterweight to 'inland is safe'. Homeowners insurance is normal here, but FLOOD is arguably worse than on parts of the coast: private flood insurance is essentially unavailable in Vermont so NFIP is the only market, and only about 7,000 NFIP policies are in force statewide at roughly $650/yr average premium. Nationally, 1 in 3 NFIP claims from 2013-2023 came from outside high-risk zones. No commute to any anchor except Burlington (~0.23M metro). Score inland subregions on FLUVIAL flood and insurance AVAILABILITY, not just on the absence of surge.
